Pennsylvania State Police Warn Businesses: Remove Skill Games by October 13

Published September 13, 2026 · 4 min read · By the OddsLighthouse Editorial Team

Pennsylvania State Police issued a formal warning to businesses this week that unlicensed skill game machines must be physically removed from their premises by October 13, not merely powered off, or owners risk seizure of the devices, confiscation of any cash inside them, and potential criminal charges. The warning applies to an estimated 70,000 machines currently operating in bars, clubs, fire halls, convenience stores, and other locations across the state.

What triggered the deadline

The warning follows a Pennsylvania Supreme Court ruling in June 2026 that found skill game machines meet the legal definition of unlicensed slot machines under the state's Gaming Act and Crimes Code, despite manufacturers' long-standing argument that an element of player skill makes the machines legally distinct from slots. The ruling included a stay of roughly 120 days to give the legislature and industry time to respond before enforcement began, and state police say that window closes October 13.

Under Pennsylvania law, only licensed casinos and certain approved truck stop locations may legally operate slot-style gaming terminals regulated by the Pennsylvania Gaming Control Board. Skill games from providers such as Pace-O-Matic, sold under names including Pennsylvania Skill, have operated for years in a legal gray area outside that licensed framework, and state police explicitly warned that simply unplugging a machine or turning it off will not be treated as compliance once the deadline passes.

Why it matters

The scale here is unusually large for a single-state enforcement action — 70,000 machines is a substantial share of Pennsylvania's small-stakes gambling landscape, spread across thousands of individual small businesses that have relied on a cut of skill-game revenue. State Rep. Russ Diamond has proposed legislation that would tax skill game revenue at 20%, with the bulk of that funding directed toward the state's Property Tax Relief Fund, as a possible legislative path to legalizing and regulating the machines rather than eliminating them outright — but no such law had passed as of this warning, leaving removal as the operative requirement for now.

For casino-industry watchers, the case is a reminder that "skill" framing has been the central legal battleground for gray-market gaming machines in several states, not just Pennsylvania, and that a state supreme court ruling against that framing can move quickly from decision to real-world enforcement once a stay expires.
